claims.claim: By the best cell counts we have, a typical man is about half human.
claims.source_checked: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLoS Biol 14(8):e1002533, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533; full text PMC4991899 via Europe PMC fullTextXML (www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4991899/fullTextXML), fetched 2026-11-18 + Hatton et al. 2023, PNAS 120(39):e2303077120, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120; full text PMC10523466 via Europe PMC fullTextXML, fetched 2026-11-18
claims.note: Sender abstract: 'We estimate the total number of bacteria in the 70 kg "reference man" to be 3.8·10^13 ... revise past estimates to 3.0·10^13 human cells'; 30/68 = 44% human. Sender: 'B/H = 1.3, with an uncertainty of 25% ... This B/H value of about 1:1'. Hatton: '≈36 trillion cells in the male' (70 kg); with Sender's bacteria 36/74 = 49%. 'Typical' is Sender's own word: 'the typical adult human body consists of about 30 trillion human cells and about 38 trillion bacteria'. 44% as 'about half' matches Sender's own 'about 1:1'. 'By ... cell counts' fixes the measure as number, not mass. 'Best ... we have' is evaluative framing; Hatton names Bianconi 2013 and Sender 2016 as the two whole-body studies 'converging on values of 30 to 37 trillion human cells', and Hatton 2023 is the newer human census; nothing newer was cited. Not true of every body (Sender Table 3: ref. woman 21 vs 44 = 32%), which is why 'typical man' must stay.

claims.claim: A4: what a viewer who swipes at 2.0 s leaves with. Heard by then: 'By the best cell counts we have,' ('have,' starts 1.670 s, 'a' 1.962 s, 'typical' 2.176 s, 'half' 3.367 s). On screen: Look 1, 68 identical neutral dots in a human outline (bacteria dots only dim from 'about'); Look 2, the unsplit Vitruvian Man with 'BY CELL COUNT' (from 'cell' minus 4 frames until 'about').
claims.source_checked: src/generated/cell-count.alignment.json (75 words; joined text identical to the script's spoken text); src/shorts/cell-count/index.tsx (Cell opacity ramps from F.less; first Tag from F.half); src/shorts/cell-count-cutout/index.tsx card 1 (Word 'BY CELL COUNT' at F.cell-4 until F.less-1; Tissue at F.half)
claims.note: At 2 s no claim has been made and nothing on screen implies one; the popular false form (10:1, '90% of your cells are bacteria') is never said or shown. A viewer who stays to the end of the first sentence (~4 s) gets 'a typical man is about half human' with 'typical 70 kg man' on screen in both looks, which both papers support (44-49%). Framing; confirmed.

claims.claim: And his passengers roughly match them, cell for cell.
claims.source_checked: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLoS Biol 14(8):e1002533, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533; full text PMC4991899 via Europe PMC fullTextXML (www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4991899/fullTextXML), fetched 2026-11-18 + Hatton et al. 2023, PNAS 120(39):e2303077120, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120; full text PMC10523466 via Europe PMC fullTextXML, fetched 2026-11-18
claims.note: The numbers are fine for the reference man: Sender 'B/H = 1.3 ... about 1:1'; 38 vs 30 (or 36, Hatton) trillion. The wording is not: 'them' points back to the previous sentence's 'your cells' (and, read closest, 'blood'), so as spoken it says the bacteria roughly match the VIEWER's cells. For Sender's reference woman that is 44 vs 21 trillion (B:H 2.2, Table 3), and against red blood cells it is 38 vs 25. This breaks the SOURCES block's own rule that 'the voice keeps to "his" for every count'. Change to a referent that is his: e.g. 'And his passengers roughly match his own cells, cell for cell.' (or '...match his own, one for one.'). Both looks' last cards already show his 30 vs 38, so only the voice needs the change.
